reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Presents in a previously healthy infant, typically in the first year of life, with prolonged febrile and afebrile hemiclonic or generalised seizures often triggered by fever, illness or vaccination
The great majority of cases are caused by loss-of-function variants in the SCN1A gene encoding a voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit
Seizures are characteristically sensitive to temperature elevation and can be precipitated by hot baths, exertion or environmental heat
Multiple seizure types emerge over the second year, including myoclonic, atypical absence, focal and atonic seizures, with a tendency to status epilepticus
Development is usually normal at onset but slows or regresses from the second year, with later intellectual disability, ataxia and behavioural difficulties
Sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure medications should generally be avoided because they typically aggravate seizures in this channelopathy
There is a heightened risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), so seizure control and safety counselling are priorities
reference.pathophysiology: Dravet syndrome is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused in most patients by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SCN1A, which encodes the Nav1.1 voltage-gated sodium channel. Nav1.1 is expressed preferentially in inhibitory GABAergic interneurons, so reduced channel function impairs interneuron firing and disinhibits cortical and hippocampal networks, producing hyperexcitability and a low threshold for seizures, particularly with rises in body temperature. The same interneuron dysfunction is thought to underlie the associated cognitive, motor and behavioural impairments that define the encephalopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+)
Other early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (e.g. KCNQ2, SCN2A)
additionalInvestigations: Targeted or panel gene testing for SCN1A and related epilepsy genes
Prolonged or video EEG, which may be normal early and later shows generalised or multifocal epileptiform discharges
Brain MRI, typically normal early but useful to exclude structural causes
Metabolic screening where an inborn error of metabolism is considered
Assessment of development and cognition to document the encephalopathic trajectory
redFlags: Prolonged or repeated febrile seizures progressing to convulsive status epilepticus
Developmental slowing or regression in the second year of life
Seizure aggravation after introduction of a sodium-channel-blocking agent
Features suggesting elevated SUDEP risk such as frequent nocturnal convulsions
reference.prognosis: Seizures typically persist into adulthood and are often drug-resistant, with associated intellectual disability, gait disturbance and behavioural problems. Mortality is elevated, largely from SUDEP and status epilepticus, so long-term multidisciplinary care and safety planning are essential.
pitfalls: Dismissing early prolonged febrile seizures as simple febrile convulsions and delaying genetic testing
Prescribing sodium-channel blockers, which commonly worsen seizures in this condition
Assuming a normal early EEG or MRI excludes the diagnosis
Overlooking fever, illness and heat as consistent seizure triggers requiring aggressive fever management
management: Base antiseizure treatment on agents effective in this syndrome, with sodium valproate and clobazam first-line and stiripentol, fenfluramine or cannabidiol added for refractory seizures
Avoid sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure drugs (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine), which aggravate seizures in this channelopathy
Provide a home rescue plan with buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam and a clear status epilepticus protocol, given the strong tendency to prolonged seizures
Minimise seizure triggers with prompt antipyresis during febrile illness and avoidance of overheating such as hot baths, while still recommending vaccination with pre-emptive fever control
Support the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with developmental therapies and management of ataxia and behavioural difficulties
Counsel on the elevated risk of SUDEP and status epilepticus and put safety and long-term multidisciplinary care planning in place
Offer clinical genetics input with SCN1A counselling and family assessment, as most cases arise de novo
